#5449. How boards investigate a CEO: 10 parts of an internal probe

Free daily briefing on global business news.

Learn how boards investigate a CEO, from special committees and outside counsel to interviews, disclosure rules and the outcomes directors can choose when an internal probe ends

Every company has one executive whom the board alone hires, pays, evaluates and can remove: the chief executive. That makes an inquiry into the CEO different from any other internal investigation. The person under review often controls the budget, the legal department and much of the information directors depend on. Corporate governance practice has developed a set of safeguards to work around that conflict.

Understanding how boards investigate a CEO starts with a familiar sequence. Independent directors take charge. They retain outside lawyers who report to them instead of to management. They write down what the inquiry will examine, lock down relevant records, interview witnesses and follow the money. At each stage, they decide what the company owes regulators, investors and the public.

Two Delaware court decisions define the legal stakes. Delaware is the state of incorporation for many large U.S. companies. Its courts expect directors to make a good-faith effort to oversee major risks. The Delaware Court of Chancery set out that oversight duty in its 1996 Caremark decision. In 2019, the Delaware Supreme Court applied it in Marchand v. Barnhill, a case arising from food safety problems at Blue Bell Creameries. Directors who overlook warning signs about a chief executive can face shareholder claims. A poorly run inquiry carries its own costs. It can put attorney-client privilege at risk, cause a company to miss a filing deadline or invite closer scrutiny from regulators.

This slideshow breaks the process into 10 parts. The first four cover who leads the probe, which lawyers do the work, how the scope is defined and how evidence is preserved. The next four explain witness interviews, forensic accounting, whistleblower complaints and the disclosure rules that apply to public companies. The final two describe how the CEO is kept out of the board's deliberations and what directors can do once the findings arrive.

The descriptions reflect common U.S. practice and established law. Bylaws, corporate charters and executive employment contracts differ from company to company. Practice varies from one investigation to the next.

Each slide is written to stand on its own. A reader interested only in Upjohn warnings, clawbacks or Form 8-K deadlines can skip directly to that entry.

When allegations reach the chief executive, a board usually assigns the inquiry to a special committee made up only of independent directors. These directors have no business, family or financial ties to the CEO. That lets them weigh the facts without a conflict of interest.

The committee can be created for the occasion or drawn from a body that already exists. The audit committee is a frequent choice when the allegations concern financial reporting. It already oversees the outside auditor and the company's internal controls. Claims about workplace conduct or personal behavior may instead go to a purpose-built committee. They can also go to the full board, meeting without the CEO.

Independence is judged by actual relationships, not only by a director's formal status. A director whom the CEO recruited may be left off the committee. The same goes for a director who serves alongside the CEO on another company's board, or one with a long personal friendship with the executive. Boards commonly ask counsel to review each prospective member's ties before the work begins.

Delaware case law gives directors reason to take care. Under the oversight duty recognized in In re Caremark International Inc. Derivative Litigation, directors must make a good-faith effort to ensure the company has information and reporting systems. The Delaware Supreme Court applied that duty in Marchand v. Barnhill, a case involving Blue Bell Creameries. The court stressed that boards must make this effort for the risks most central to the business. Shareholders can bring derivative claims against directors who fail to meet that duty.

A committee needs formal authority as well as independent members. A board resolution, often called the committee's charter, gives it the power to hire its own advisers. The same document lets it demand company records and speak with any employee. It also sets the reporting line, which in most cases runs to the full board minus the CEO.

The choice of committee leader carries weight. A lead independent director or a non-executive chair often acts as the main contact for the outside lawyers. That arrangement keeps the CEO and other senior managers out of the chain of communication. It also helps shield the inquiry from accusations of interference by the executive under review.

A special committee investigating a CEO hires its own outside law firm. That firm takes instructions from the committee rather than from the chief executive or anyone in management. The separate reporting line gives regulators, auditors and shareholders a reason to trust what the investigation finds.

Boards generally avoid the company's regular outside law firm for this work. A firm that earns large fees from routine corporate matters can look like it has a stake in the result. So can a firm whose partners deal with the CEO regularly. Committees tend to pick a firm with no history of advising the executive under review. They also run a conflicts check on the firm's other clients before signing.

The engagement letter names the committee as the party the lawyers answer to. That wording helps support attorney-client privilege. The privilege can shield confidential communications between a lawyer and a client from disclosure in later lawsuits. It belongs to the company itself. In this setting, the committee typically decides on the company's behalf whether to keep it or give it up.

The protection can be lost. Handing findings to a government agency or another outside party may lead a court to rule that privilege has been waived for that material. Some committees ask for oral briefings instead of a long written report for that reason. Others want a document they can share with regulators and accept the waiver risk that comes with it.

Investigation teams at these firms often include former federal prosecutors. Those lawyers know how the Justice Department and the Securities and Exchange Commission judge whether a company's internal inquiry was independent and thorough. The firm can also bring in specialists, such as e-discovery vendors, and supervise their work.

The company pays the legal bills. That puts the CEO's own organization in the position of funding an inquiry into its leader. Committees handle the problem by approving the fee terms themselves and having invoices sent straight to them. Management has no role in setting the budget or signing off on the bills.

Counsel also guides the committee's process from the first meeting. The lawyers advise on the order of steps, how to document decisions and when to brief the outside auditor or regulators. That record can matter later if a court or agency examines how the board handled the matter.

Before any witness is interviewed, the special committee puts the scope of a CEO investigation in writing. That mandate names the allegations under review, the time period covered, the people and records involved and the authority the investigators hold.

The document is usually a committee resolution, an engagement letter with outside counsel or both. Its terms need to be precise. An allegation that the CEO misused a company aircraft calls for different records and witnesses than an allegation of harassment. Pressure on the finance team to hit a quarterly target would call for yet another set.

A defined scope also keeps the inquiry from drifting. A review of expense reports can surface questions about related-party deals or a vendor contract. Each new thread adds cost and time. With a written mandate in hand, the committee can choose to widen the inquiry, keep it narrow or open a separate review with its own terms.

The mandate states who receives the findings. In most cases that is the special committee, which then decides what to pass to the full board. The document can bar the CEO from receiving drafts. Counsel still reviews the executive's employment agreement and the company's bylaws. Either one may grant the CEO a right to information or a chance to respond.

Access is another core term. A typical mandate gives the investigators authority to reach any employee, any company system and any document the business holds. It also directs management to cooperate. Corporate codes of conduct and employment contracts often require staff to assist internal inquiries, and the mandate can cite those obligations.

The document also covers unexpected discoveries. Investigators may find signs of a separate problem, such as possible bribery or an accounting error. The mandate can require them to alert the committee at once. The committee then decides whether to bring in other advisers or notify the outside auditor.

A mandate is not fixed. When the facts change, the committee amends the scope in writing. Each expansion or narrowing then appears in the record as a deliberate decision rather than an accident.

That record has a later use. The company may face shareholder litigation or questions from regulators. A written mandate and dated committee minutes show what the committee asked for, when it asked and why.

Locking down evidence is the first concrete step in a CEO investigation. Early in the process, the company sends a legal hold notice telling employees to keep relevant records intact. Its IT team also switches off the routine deletion of email, files and chat history.

The chief executive's own data comes first. Investigators move early to secure the CEO's company email, calendar, phone, laptop and cloud accounts. A common method is a forensic image, which is a complete copy of a device's contents made in a way that can be verified later. A copy taken at the outset makes it harder for anyone to argue afterward that material was altered or removed.

Personal phones and messaging apps are harder to reach. Executives may conduct business over text messages, WhatsApp or Signal. Some of these apps can be set to erase messages after a period of time. The U.S. Department of Justice addressed this problem in March 2023, when it updated its Evaluation of Corporate Compliance Programs. The revision covers how companies govern personal devices, communication platforms and messaging applications, including those that make messages ephemeral.

Losing data carries legal consequences. Federal Rule of Civil Procedure 37(e) deals with electronically stored information that should have been kept but was lost. If a party failed to take reasonable steps to preserve it, a court can order measures to cure the resulting harm. Where the loss was intended to deprive another party of the information, the court can impose harsher sanctions. Those include instructing a jury that the lost information was unfavorable to the party that lost it, or dismissing the case.

The hold notice goes to a defined group known as custodians — the people likely to hold relevant records. In a CEO probe, that list usually starts with the executive, direct reports and assistants. It then extends to finance staff and others involved in the matters under review. Counsel adds names as interviews and documents point to other people who handled the material.

Records generated by company systems matter as much as messages. Access logs, badge swipes and expense approval trails show who acted and when. Investigators use them to test what witnesses say against what the systems recorded. Some systems overwrite their logs on a rotating schedule. The hold covers them for that reason.

Collection follows preservation. E-discovery vendors process the gathered data into a searchable form. Lawyers then search it using keywords, names and date ranges drawn from the scope of the investigation.

Outside counsel typically opens each witness interview in a CEO investigation with an Upjohn warning. The lawyer tells the employee that counsel represents the company, not the individual, and that the company controls the privilege over the conversation.

The warning is named for Upjohn Co. v. United States, a 1981 U.S. Supreme Court decision. The Court held that attorney-client privilege can protect conversations between a company's lawyers and its employees. The protection applies when those conversations help the lawyers give legal advice to the company. The Court rejected a narrower "control group" test, which had limited the privilege to senior managers. That ruling lets investigators question staff well below the executive suite and still treat the exchanges as privileged.

The warning is sometimes nicknamed a "corporate Miranda," although it is not a constitutional right. Its job is to prevent a misunderstanding. An employee who assumes the company's lawyer is also a personal lawyer may speak more freely than intended. A later claim that a personal attorney-client relationship existed can cloud the company's control over the interview.

A standard warning covers a handful of points. The lawyer works for the company. The conversation is confidential. The company can waive the privilege and share the employee's statements with regulators or prosecutors without the employee's consent. Counsel usually confirms that the employee understands before asking about the facts.

An employee who wants personal advice can hire a separate lawyer. Some companies pay for that representation under their bylaws or an indemnification agreement.

The order of interviews follows a pattern. Counsel generally reviews documents first and then speaks with people on the edges of the events. Witnesses closer to the conduct come next. The CEO is often interviewed near the end. By then, the lawyers can test the executive's account against emails, records and other testimony.

Interviews are usually not recorded or transcribed. Lawyers take notes and write memoranda that reflect their own impressions and analysis. That approach can strengthen work-product protection for the materials. The memoranda summarize rather than quote, and witnesses do not usually sign them.

Counsel often reminds employees that company policy forbids retaliation for taking part. Witnesses are also asked not to discuss the interview with colleagues. That request helps keep later accounts independent. It cannot stop an employee from reporting possible violations to the Securities and Exchange Commission, which bars companies from impeding such communications.

The CEO occupies a different position as the subject of the probe. The executive can bring a personal lawyer and may negotiate the timing and format of the interview. The special committee decides whether to insist on a face-to-face session or accept a written response.

Forensic accountants trace where company money went in a CEO investigation. They examine expense reports, wire transfers, vendor payments and sign-off records. The goal is to test whether spending followed company policy and whether the required approvals were actually given.

Their work starts with specific questions. Were the chief executive's travel and entertainment claims backed by receipts? Did company money reach vendors connected to the executive or to family members? Were contracts broken into smaller pieces to slip under approval limits? Did anyone override a control, and who was aware of it?

To answer those questions, the accountants line up ledger entries against bank statements, invoices and email. A payment recorded in the books with no matching invoice becomes a lead for the lawyers. So does a spending approval that cannot be traced to the person who was supposed to give it.

Data analytics widens the search. Software can sort through large volumes of transactions to flag duplicate payments, round-number entries, payments made at unusual times and money sent to new vendors. None of those patterns proves misconduct by itself. Each one points investigators toward documents to pull and witnesses to question.

Related-party transactions draw close scrutiny in an inquiry focused on a chief executive. These are deals between the company and an insider, or someone close to an insider. U.S. public companies must disclose some of these arrangements in their securities filings. A deal that was left out or described inaccurately can become a reporting problem separate from the original allegation.

The accounting firm is usually hired by outside counsel rather than by the company directly. That structure draws on United States v. Kovel, a 1961 decision by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Second Circuit. The court recognized that attorney-client privilege can extend to an accountant who helps a lawyer understand financial information in order to give legal advice. Whether the protection holds in a given case depends on how the engagement is set up and used.

The company's outside auditor plays a different part. The auditor stays independent of the investigation. It may still ask what the board's special committee has found. Alleged executive misconduct can affect the auditor's view of management's integrity and of the financial statements. The committee and its lawyers decide when and how the auditor is briefed.

The accountants' conclusions flow into the committee's final report. They put a dollar figure on the amounts at issue. They also help directors distinguish a policy breach from an accounting error or an intentional scheme.

Many CEO investigations begin with a tip, such as a hotline report, an employee complaint or a letter sent directly to a director. U.S. law requires listed companies to keep a channel open for these reports, and it protects the people who use it.

The Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 gave that job to the audit committee. Audit committees of listed companies must set procedures for receiving, keeping and handling complaints about accounting, internal controls and auditing. Employees must be able to raise those concerns confidentially and anonymously. Many companies hire an outside vendor to run the hotline.

Section 806 of the same law addresses retaliation. It protects public-company employees who report conduct they reasonably believe is fraud or a securities law violation. A worker who is fired or demoted after reporting can file a complaint with the U.S. Department of Labor's Occupational Safety and Health Administration within 180 days. Boards that receive a complaint typically document how the complainant is treated from the first day.

The Dodd-Frank Act of 2010 opened a second path. Its whistleblower program lets the Securities and Exchange Commission pay tipsters a share of what it recovers. Awards run from 10 percent to 30 percent of money collected in actions with sanctions above $1 million. An employee can go to the agency at the same time as the board, or without telling the board at all.

The agency's rules reward internal reporting without requiring it. A whistleblower who reports inside the company and then contacts the agency within 120 days can be treated as having reported on the date of the internal complaint. The agency's Rule 21F-17 bars anyone from taking steps to impede a person from communicating directly with agency staff about a possible securities law violation. That ban covers enforcing or threatening to enforce a confidentiality agreement.

The practical result is that a board does not fully control the timeline. A committee that receives a credible tip moves quickly and records when the information arrived. It avoids any step that could look like an effort to unmask or silence the source.

Routing is the first decision. A complaint that names the CEO or the general counsel should bypass both and go straight to independent directors, usually starting with the audit committee chair. That director judges whether the allegation, if true, is serious enough to warrant an independent probe. Investigators typically speak with the complainant early. They protect the person's identity as far as the law and the facts permit.

A public company does not have to announce an internal investigation of its CEO when the inquiry begins. Certain outcomes do trigger fast reporting. If the chief executive leaves, the company generally must file a Form 8-K with the Securities and Exchange Commission (SEC) within four business days.

Form 8-K is the SEC's current report for major corporate events. The governing provision for a CEO exit is Item 5.02. It covers the departure of directors and certain senior officers, including the principal executive officer. The filing must state that the executive resigned, retired or was terminated, along with the date. A reason is not required. If the company chooses to give one, that description has to be accurate and not misleading.

The same item covers the other side of a leadership change. When the board appoints a new principal executive officer, Item 5.02 calls for a filing on that appointment too.

Financial findings carry a deadline of their own. The board or audit committee may conclude that previously issued financial statements should no longer be relied on. Item 4.02 of Form 8-K then requires a filing within four business days. A probe into executive spending or revenue practices can lead to that conclusion.

Staying quiet about an inquiry still carries legal risk. Rule 10b-5, adopted under the Securities Exchange Act of 1934, bars materially false statements. It also bars omitting facts needed to keep other statements from being misleading. A company that praises its leadership while aware of serious allegations can expose itself to liability. Counsel reviews earnings releases, filings and executive remarks with that risk in view.

Executive certifications add pressure. Sections 302 and 906 of the Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 require the CEO and chief financial officer to certify the company's periodic reports. When an investigation casts doubt on those reports, the committee, the outside auditor and disclosure counsel assess whether the earlier statements still hold.

Reporting to authorities is a separate decision from public disclosure. A company may choose to tell the SEC or the U.S. Department of Justice about possible violations. The Justice Department has published corporate enforcement policies describing credit for voluntary self-disclosure, cooperation and remediation. The board weighs that option with its lawyers.

Stock exchange rules also apply. The New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq $NDAQ expect listed companies to release material news promptly. A CEO exit or a restatement can meet that standard.

A small group controls the message. The committee, outside counsel and the corporate secretary agree on what is said to employees and the public. Conflicting accounts can create legal problems of their own.

During an internal investigation, the chief executive is cut out of every decision about the probe. The CEO does not attend special committee meetings, does not see the committee's papers and has no say over the investigating lawyers. In many cases, the executive continues to run the business day to day.

The arrangement is harder to manage when one person is both CEO and board chair. In that case, the lead independent director or another independent director chosen by the board presides over any discussion of the inquiry. The chair's usual control over meeting agendas and board materials does not extend to the investigation.

Listed companies already have a forum for these conversations. New York Stock Exchange rules require non-management directors to meet in regularly scheduled executive sessions without management present. Nasdaq $NDAQ rules require regularly scheduled executive sessions of independent directors. Those meetings give directors a routine place to discuss the probe without the executive in the room.

Recusal covers votes as well as attendance. The chief executive abstains from any board decision about the investigation, including its budget and its conclusions. The general counsel may also have a conflict. That officer usually reports to the CEO. Committees often limit the general counsel's role to logistics, or keep the general counsel out of the inquiry entirely.

Directors also decide how the executive will operate while the work continues. One choice is a leave of absence. Another is to remove the CEO's authority over particular areas, such as the finance function or the employees being interviewed. A third is to make no change when the allegations are narrow. The committee weighs the risk of interference against disruption to the company.

The executive keeps rights during the process. A CEO under investigation can hire a personal lawyer and is normally given a chance to answer the allegations. Company bylaws, indemnification agreements and employment contracts can determine whether the company covers legal costs as they arise. Section 145 of the Delaware General Corporation Law permits companies to advance those expenses to officers. The officer typically must promise to repay the money if a court later finds the officer is not entitled to indemnification.

Succession planning runs on a separate track. Directors identify who could serve as interim CEO and how operations would stay stable if the executive leaves. That discussion is kept apart from the fact-finding. The separation keeps choices about a possible replacement from shaping the investigation's conclusions.

The rest of the board stays informed. The committee briefs the other independent directors at intervals. Those updates let the full board carry out its own oversight duties.

At the end of a CEO investigation, the special committee presents its findings and the independent directors decide how to respond. The options range from clearing the executive entirely to firing the CEO for cause. Reprimands, pay cuts and compensation recovery fall in between.

The CEO's employment agreement usually sets the boundaries of that decision. Many executive contracts define cause to include conduct such as fraud, willful misconduct or serious breaches of company policy. A dismissal for cause can cost the executive severance and unvested equity. Directors and counsel therefore test the facts against the contract's exact wording. Labeling a departure as for cause when the evidence does not meet the definition can lead to a dispute with the former executive.

Recovering pay is a separate track. The Securities and Exchange Commission adopted Rule 10D-1 under the Dodd-Frank Act. It requires listed companies to keep policies for clawing back incentive-based compensation that executives received in error because of an accounting restatement. The New York Stock Exchange and Nasdaq $NDAQ put the rule into effect through their listing standards. Companies had to adopt compliant policies by December 2023.

Rule 10D-1 has a narrow trigger. A restatement sets it off, not misconduct in general. Recovery applies whether or not the executive was at fault. It covers current and former executive officers. It reaches incentive pay received during the three completed fiscal years before the restatement was required. A CEO who broke conduct rules without affecting the financial statements falls outside it.

The Sarbanes-Oxley Act of 2002 contains an older recovery provision. Section 304 covers the CEO and the chief financial officer when misconduct leads to a restatement. It reaches bonuses, incentive pay and profits from selling company stock in the 12 months after the misstated filing. The SEC enforces it, not the board.

Company-written clawback clauses can go further. Depending on how they are drafted and what the executive signed, they may reach compensation tied to misconduct. Collecting the money can still require negotiation or a lawsuit.

The committee's conclusions go to the independent directors, who weigh them before voting on any action. Their reasoning belongs in the board minutes. Those minutes become the formal record of how the company handled the allegations.

Remediation follows the decision about the CEO. Committees often order changes to the controls, approval limits or reporting lines that allowed the problem. A documented record of those fixes can matter if regulators later examine how the board responded.

Not every probe ends with a finding against the executive. When the evidence does not support the allegations, the committee says so in its conclusions. The board then records that it has cleared the CEO. That written record shows directors examined the allegations and acted on what the evidence showed.

#5448. ‘The easiest way to penetrate a billion-dollar company’: Ex-FBI operative on how spies target CEOs

Jensen Huang’s exit from Nvidia has put a rarely discussed risk in plain view: for a CEO, a new business contact or a budding romance may come from someone more interested in the company’s secrets.

“Sometimes the easiest way to penetrate a billion-dollar company is to get close to the person running it,” Eric O’Neill, a former FBI counterintelligence operative, told Fortune.

For O’Neill, protecting executives should include teaching them to recognize manipulation—and giving others a way to intervene when the boss won’t listen.

Huang stepped down Thursday as president, CEO, and a board member of Nvidia, No. 16 on the 2026 Fortune 500, amid scrutiny of his relationship with a woman suspected of spying for China. The company named chief financial officer Colette Kress interim CEO while its board searches for a permanent successor.

In a message to employees Sunday, Huang acknowledged being unfaithful to his wife and said he would cooperate with the board’s investigation. The New York Times reported that U.S. intelligence officials believed Alice Huang, a former executive at Singapore-based Megaspeed, had been recruited by China’s intelligence service. The Chinese government has denied the allegations.

Nvidia’s board said Sunday that it had no reason to believe company secrets or national security had been compromised, but that its independent investigation, led by a committee of independent directors, would examine all available information. The company has lost about $450 billion in market value since Huang’s admission.

O’Neill, whose undercover work helped catch FBI spy Robert Hanssen, founded NeXasure AI and wrote Spies, Lies, and Cybercrime. He said an intelligence-gathering attempt often looks, at first, like an ordinary relationship.

He said an approach rarely begins with someone asking an executive to hand over company secrets. It may start at a conference, through a business introduction, over drinks, or even on a dating app. The operative finds common ground, builds trust, and makes the executive feel important.

Romance can speed things up. Using romantic or sexual interest to gain information, access, or leverage is known as “honey trapping,” a tactic far older than dating apps.

The warning signs can be subtle, O’Neill said: a relationship that moves unusually quickly, persistent questions about sensitive business matters, requests to meet influential colleagues, or encouragement to keep secrets. The goal may be information, influence over a business decision, or compromising material that could later be used for blackmail.

Those signs are harder to recognize when the person under scrutiny is someone the executive trusts.

“By the time a security professional raises concerns, the executive may already be emotionally invested and unwilling to listen,” O’Neill said.

CEOs have access to information others want, from intellectual property and strategic plans to government relationships. O’Neill argues their security training should teach them how someone might use a personal relationship to get closer to those assets.

Peter Warmka, a former CIA senior intelligence officer who now trains executives through his Counterintelligence Institute, told Fortune his sessions cover who might target a company, what they want, and how they approach employees and contractors. Senior executives are prime targets because of their access, he said, but their attitudes toward security can also leave them exposed.

“Unfortunately, they are also perceived as more vulnerable because many believe not all security measures imposed on lower-level employees also apply to them,” Warmka said.

Much of his training focuses on overseas travel, including the risks of electronic eavesdropping in hotel rooms and on the way to meetings, intelligence collection targeting their devices, and interpreters who may work for intelligence services.

Even with that preparation, recognizing an attempt to extract information can be difficult. “Well-trained operatives know how to elicit information without raising suspicion,” Warmka said.

When a CEO dismisses a warning, someone else needs a way to act.

Chief security officers, general counsel, and chief information security officers should have a confidential route to independent directors, O’Neill said. If the CEO will not cooperate, the board can bring in outside counsel and investigators to assess a credible threat and recommend protective measures. Where warranted, the company should involve federal authorities.

“No executive, regardless of wealth, reputation, or brilliance, should be the final authority on investigating a threat in which that executive may be personally compromised,” O’Neill said.

Tatiana Sataua is a News Fellow at Fortune covering business, technology, AI, and consumer culture.

#5446. Scott Bessent says Treasury wanted to blacklist Megaspeed ‘for months,’ blaming Howard Lutnick as Nvidia fallout widens: ‘Commerce has the pen’

Secretary of Commerce Howard Lutnick is now facing public pressure from his fellow Cabinet members over his decision to not blacklist Megaspeed, the cloud computing company at the center of Nvidia ex-CEO Jensen Huang’s affair with a suspected Chinese spy.

The Treasury Department, among other federal agencies, were in favor of placing trade restrictions on Megaspeed, but the decision ultimately lay with Lutnick, Treasury Secretary Scott Bessent told CNBC on Friday.

“There was coordination. Treasury, War, USTR, and State were in favor of putting Megaspeed on the entity list for months,” he said. “But Commerce has the pen….You will have to ask them about their internal processes.”

Megaspeed is under investigation by the Justice Department over the suspected violation of U.S. export controls, which prohibit certain U.S.-made chips from being sold and shipped to China. Helmed by Alice Huang, the alleged spy, Megaspeed and its Malaysian subsidiary Speedmatric shipped at least $7.5 billion in Nvidia chips to China over two years, The Information reported.

Lutnick is facing intensifying scrutiny over reports he took action to protect Nvidia from the Trump administration’s export controls of U.S. AI hardware to China. The commerce secretary reportedly spent months “undoing” efforts to hold Megaspeed accountable for potential export control violations, Axios reported. Bessent confronted Lutnick in the Situation Room following the midterm elections over not placing Megaspeed on the entity list, according to the outlet.

Bessent told CNBC, “We don’t repeat conversations in the Situation Room.”

According to the New York Times, when Trump officials approached Oracle about cancelling a $7 billion deal to lease chips to Chinese tech conglomerate Tencent, Lutnick’s top deputy Jeff Kessler spoke up and said Lutnick had issues with a cancellation, as it would halt the shipment of 100,000 advanced Nvidia AI chips. Lutnick reportedly said he didn’t understand the rush to scrap the deal.

The Commerce Department and Nvidia did not immediately respond to Fortune’s request for comment.

Both Republican and Democratic lawmakers want to hold Lutnick accountable for not placing Megaspeed on the blacklist.

“The obvious question is why did he choose to sell advanced chips?” Republican Louisiana Sen. John Kennedy told Politico. “Secretary Lutnick needs to answer that in front of God and country.”

Lutnick agreed to testify alongside Huang before the Senate Banking Committee to address national security concerns on Dec. 10.

Meanwhile, senior White House officials are now weighing whether to oust the commerce secretary from his position, Reuters reported. Even before news of Huang’s affair broke, Lutnick’s decision not to add 100 companies, including China’s DeekSeek, to the entity list put him in hot water.

Lutnick argued with senior White House officials that export regulations against China would stoke the trade war with China and he insisted on having conversations with Trump about China’s restricted access to U.S. chips, the Times reported.

The commerce secretary also had a friendly relationship and financial ties with Nvidia, bolstering concerns about favoritism toward the tech company.

“Howard is the person I talk to most in the administration—he’s on top of the technology and learning the industry quickly,” Huang said in September 2025.

Before Lutnick became commerce secretary, he was the CEO and chairman of investment bank Cantor Fitzgerald, which held about $1.2 billion in Nvidia stock prior to President Donald Trump’s second term.

Sasha Rogelberg is a reporter and former editorial fellow on the news desk at Fortune, covering retail and the intersection of business and popular culture.

#5445. AWS gives developers a free local stand-in for its cloud, built from scratch by AI agents

by Todd Bishop on Nov 11, 2026 at 10:51 amNovember 11, 2026 at 10:51 am

AWS says its engineers didn’t write or review a single line of code in its newest developer tool, and the company is touting that as a selling point.

AWS Emulator, released Wednesday, simulates AWS services on a developer’s own machine. It’s built from more than 400 API models covering more than 200 AWS services. Developers and AI coding agents can use it to test code without a network connection and without paying for the real cloud.

The tool addresses a problem that coding agents such as Amazon’s Kiro and Anthropic’s Claude Code have made worse. Agents can write code faster than teams can test it against the real cloud. Agents check their work by running the code and reading the results, over and over, and doing that in the cloud adds delays and costs.

The emulator lets them run that loop on a developer’s own machine.

In an ironic or perhaps appropriate twist, AWS used AI agents to build the emulator. Agents also maintain it, testing it against real AWS and fixing the gaps they find.

“The emulator was written entirely by autonomous agents. Our team hasn’t written or reviewed any of the code,” wrote Matt Goldberg, the AWS senior principal engineer behind the project, in a blog post.

Goldberg compared his agents to himself as a kindergartner, too young to hold a crayon properly, who got yelled at by classmates for ruining a group drawing of dinosaurs. The problem wasn’t bad intent, he wrote, just a lack of competence. The answer, for agents, is clearly defined areas to fill in.

“I think agents also need coloring books,” he wrote.

The agents work from AWS’s public API models, which describe how each service should behave, and check their work against the real AWS cloud.

The agents run on Amazon Bedrock AgentCore in three teams. One writes “fidelity tests” — real-world scenarios such as creating a queue, sending a message and deleting the queue — and checks each against real AWS. A second runs those tests against the emulator and files issues for failures, and a third fixes them, one agent per issue.

Every change passes through an automated gate where other agents check coding standards and security. Goldberg wrote that hundreds of agents now fix thousands of issues a day.

The project started as a weekend experiment, inspired by Anthropic’s demonstration earlier this year in which a team of Claude agents built a C compiler. Goldberg gave Kiro a three-step prompt and got a passable first version of Amazon SQS, AWS’s message queuing service, in 15 minutes.

By the end of the weekend, Goldberg wrote, Kiro had built a rough version of the rest of AWS, with obvious gaps, and his team started using it to test its software that Monday.

Swami Sivasubramanian, AWS vice president of agentic AI and emerging tech, tied the project to a lesson he described to GeekWire in June. He spent four nights babysitting Kiro as it tried to rebuild a replication engine he and Allan Vermeulen built by hand nearly 20 years ago.

Once he gave the agent a spec and a way to test its work, the job took about two hours.

“When agents write the code and check their own work, the engineer’s job is to give them room to work on their own and to build the specs, tests, and merge gates that decide when that work is correct,” Sivasubramanian wrote in a guest post on CTO Werner Vogels’ blog.

It’s the same idea behind Amazon’s recent move to rewrite its engineering playbook for an era when AI writes the code.

The emulator has limits. Devin Pratt, an IDC analyst, told InfoWorld that it doesn’t yet simulate throttling, outages or differences in which services and features are available by region, and that it doesn’t sandbox the code it runs. The agents’ backlog of known gaps is public, in a GitHub folder called “things-that-do-not-work.”

Other AWS emulators exist, most notably LocalStack, which this year put its free version behind an account requirement and limited it to noncommercial use. AWS released its emulator for free under CC0, a public domain dedication, with the full commit history on GitHub.

The company says it will share more at its upcoming re:Invent conference.

#5444. Exclusive: OpenAI disbands its stand-alone robotics team as its general models start running robots

OpenAI has disbanded its stand-alone robotics team, moving its researchers onto other teams.The company confirmed the reorganization when asked about it by Fortune. A company spokesperson said that robotics remains a core part of OpenAI’s long-term vision and portrayed the reorganization as a sign of the company’s commitment to robotics, rather than a retreat from it.OpenAI said it has reassigned its robotics research team to the company’s main research team, reporting to Chief Research Officer Mark Chen, while the applied robotics and hardware teams have been reassigned to the company’s larger Applied organization, which reports to OpenAI President Greg Brockman.The change came recently enough that OpenAI had already registered a booth at CoRL, a top academic robotics conference in Austin, this week. Though the conference app and floor plan marked OpenAI’s spot, when Fortune visited booth #208, it sat empty with OpenAI’s logo nowhere to be seen.

OpenAI had a robotics team in its early days but wound it down in 2020, with cofounder Wojciech Zaremba later citing limited robot data and a more efficient path toward artificial general intelligence (AGI)—the human-like AI that has been OpenAI’s goal since its founding—through other methods. In particular, OpenAI became increasingly devoted to training ultra-large language models on vast datasets of human-written text. This is the approach that eventually yielded the company’s breakthrough product ChatGPT in late 2022.OpenAI rebuilt a stand alone robotics team in 2024, announcing a partnership with the startup Figure to develop AI models for humanoid robots. That partnership ended in February 2025, when Figure said it would develop its own robot AI. OpenAI has said it is currently developing its own humanoid robot, with CEO Sam Altman targeting a first public demonstration in 2027. The company spokesperson said that despite the reorganization, OpenAI remains committed to bringing general-purpose robots into the world.The reorganization reflects a bet that is gaining traction across the AI industry: that general-purpose models built for language, code, and vision can also be used for “embodied AI”—where AI models control devices that can act in the physical world, such as robots, driverless cars, or drones. This would obviate the need to have separate robotics teams building specialized AI models just to be the digital “brains” for robots.Researchers have seen surprising performance when connecting GPT-6 Astra to robots, directly using the general-purpose AI model to perform some robotic tasks.Guanya Shi, an assistant professor at Carnegie Mellon University’s Robotics Institute, reacted to the change at OpenAI, telling Fortune that he would interpret the move as a signal that OpenAI sees robotics as “no longer a special problem.” Instead, he said, they likely see robotics as a challenge that can be addressed as a downstream application of general intelligence—similar to the way the same underlying frontier AI models now power specialized coding tools, or tools for legal or financial work.OpenAI seemed to confirm this view in its response to Fortune. It said that at the start of the year, the company’s researchers assumed the best way to make progress on robotics was to build on its work on AI models such as Sora, a video generation model that, in order to create realistic videos, had to have some implicit understanding of how the physical world works.But since then, the company spokesperson said, the company’s general-purpose frontier models, including GPT-6 Astra, have shown that can be directly applied to robotics. This discovery is what motivated OpenAI to disband the stand alone robotics team and move the affiliated researchers onto teams working on more general AI models.The reorganization also comes at a time when OpenAI is under pressure to rein in its costs and show that it is more focused on a few, core products. Last year, Altman told the company that it needed to abandon “side quests,” and the company has jettisoned some efforts—including Sora—in order to reallocate computing resources to more core and potentially-profitable endeavors. The company is under pressure to stanch its heavy operating losses—which reportedly totaled $10.9 billion in the most recent quarter—as it seeks to close a new funding round and prepares for a possible IPO in early 2027.

This line of thinking—that general AI models can be applied directly to controlling robots without the need to create specialized models with “spatial intelligence”—would seem to challenge the assumptions underpinning many of today’s robotics startups, which have raised billions on the premise that robots need brains of their own.

But Russ Tedrake, an MIT professor and cofounder and CEO of Walden Robotics, said robotics companies still have an advantage the AI labs don’t: Their robots are already gaining work experience in real places, such as on factory floors. Such “deployment” experience—and the data these robots gather—helps robots adapt to specific workplaces and tasks. Better foundational models make that site-specific data more valuable because robots can learn from it faster, Tedrake said.

Recent experiments have tested how much work a general-purpose model can do without specialized training on robotic data. Researchers gave Astra camera images, robot information and a control interface that allowed the model to command the robot to take certain actions. In an Nvidia study, an Astra-powered agent achieved a 74.8% success rate on a simulated manipulation benchmark—where the model commands a simulated robot in a digital simulation, as opposed to a real robot—compared with 51.0% reported by the best specialized robotic models on this leaderboard.

Shi said advances in general models’ spatial and reasoning capabilities already let them handle tasks that previously required dedicated training. They can cope when a bottle is in a different position or the lighting changes, and reason about the sequence of a task or which step went wrong, he said.

Meanwhile, large language models are powerful but slow and need to be hosted in the cloud, meaning the robot or device needs a constant network connection. Shi still sees a need for smaller, specialized models that can run on a robot’s onboard computer without needing a constant internet connection.

“There may be different starting points for how to grow intelligence,” Pete Florence, cofounder of Generalist, a startup training general-purpose AI models for robots, told Fortune. He said it was unclear that any existing model would be the one that dominates robotics in the long-run.For its part, OpenAI said it was reassigning its robotics researchers to other teams because it now believes this is the best way to accelerate progress towards building general-purpose robots.

Back at booth #208 at CoRL, a few former members of the once-unified, stand-alone OpenAI robotics team milled about. They still drew a crowd, despite having no display or demo. After all, one of the conference’s hottest questions was how much robotics expertise would remain valuable as general-purpose models grew more capable—and the experience of those former OpenAI robotics researchers, now dispatched to other teams, offered one answer. Update, Nov. 13: This story has been updated to clarify the status of the OpenAI robotics team members who were at CoRL.

Wen Shao is a reporting fellow at Fortune covering AI, with a focus on the companies, economics, and infrastructure shaping the industry.

#5443. Your Customers Are Asking AI About Your Company. Here’s How to Audit What It Says.

You're viewing the US website. Looking for the Site edition?

AI is changing how customers research businesses. CEOs need this eight-step, modern reputation audit to figure out what customers are seeing.

Opinions expressed by Entrepreneur contributors are their own.

Your customers can now investigate your company without visiting your website or clicking a traditional search result.

They can ask an AI platform to compare your company with competitors, summarize customer complaints, research your leadership and identify potential reasons not to do business with you. The resulting answer can shape an opinion before the customer reaches your website.

That changes what CEOs need to monitor. Google results, news coverage, reviews and social media still matter, but an online reputation audit in 2026 should also examine what AI platforms say about your business, which sources support those answers and whether inaccurate or outdated information keeps appearing.

Google reported this year that AI Overviews had more than 2.5 billion monthly active users and AI Mode had surpassed 1 billion monthly users. CEOs should account for this behavior in the same way they learned to pay attention to Google results and online reviews.

I work in online reputation management, and at my company Reputation Pros, we recommend treating a reputation audit as a recurring business process. You do not need sophisticated software to start. You just need the right questions and a system for recording what you find. Here is an audit I recommend.

Typing your company name into an AI platform will not tell you enough. Instead, put yourself in the position of a prospective customer conducting due diligence. Ask questions that require the platform to explain what it knows about your company.

Start by copying and customizing this prompt: “I’m considering doing business with [COMPANY NAME]. Research its online reputation as a prospective customer would. Summarize what the company is known for, common positive themes, recurring complaints or criticisms, significant controversies and information that could reasonably affect a customer’s decision. Separate verified facts from allegations or opinions. Where possible, identify the sources supporting each important claim and flag information that may be outdated or uncertain.”

Run the same prompt through several major AI platforms. Do not focus solely on whether the answers sound positive or negative. Look for patterns.

Does the same complaint appear several times? Does one platform emphasize an old controversy? Does another describe your company incorrectly? Which publications, review sites or other sources appear repeatedly?

Record the results. One response does not define your reputation. Differences between platforms can show you where additional investigation is necessary.

CEOs naturally focus on branded searches, but customers do not always begin there. Someone looking for a financial adviser, attorney, software company or home services provider may start by asking for reputable companies in a particular market. The customer may then compare two or three businesses before searching any company individually.

Test that part of the journey too. Use questions such as:

Pay attention to how your company appears in those answers. Do not assume that an omission means something is wrong. Instead, investigate whether credible online sources clearly establish the expertise, history and services your company claims.

This exercise can reveal a problem that a branded Google search will miss: The information people find about your company may look fine, while the broader information environment barely associates your company with the category you want to lead.

Customers are not the only people conducting online research. Potential employees, investors, vendors and business partners can investigate company leadership before making decisions. A CEO’s online reputation deserves its own audit.

Try this: “Research [CEO’S NAME] as if you were a potential business partner conducting due diligence. Summarize their professional background, current business affiliations, documented accomplishments, controversies, lawsuits or regulatory matters and recurring criticism. Distinguish verified facts from allegations and opinions. Identify the sources supporting significant claims and flag information that appears outdated, conflicting or uncertain.”

Check the basic facts first. Is the current position correct? Are former positions described as current? Are business affiliations accurate? Does the answer confuse the CEO with someone who has a similar name?

Do not ignore an error because it happens to make the CEO look good. An inaccurate award, inflated job title or incorrect company affiliation can create credibility problems just as easily as negative misinformation.

Executives sometimes see an unfavorable result and immediately ask how to remove it. Ask whether it is accurate first.

I use five simple classifications when examining reputation issues:

Those categories force you to distinguish between information that damages your reputation and information that you simply dislike.

A legitimate negative customer review requires a different response from a false claim about your company. An accurate article from six years ago requires a different approach from a biography that incorrectly lists an executive’s former employer.

AI can help organize this part of the audit. Copy a concerning response and ask: “Extract every factual claim in the following response that can be independently verified. Organize the claims by Claim, Source Cited, Verification Needed and Potential Business Impact. Do not assume a claim is accurate because it appears in the response.”

Then verify the important claims yourself using reliable sources. Do not use one AI system to declare another AI system correct. Use AI to identify what needs checking. Use primary and authoritative sources to determine what is true.

An unfavorable AI answer is often the symptom rather than the underlying problem. Investigate the sources behind it.

You may discover an outdated executive biography, an old news article, incorrect directory information, inconsistent company descriptions or customer complaints appearing across multiple sites. Ask the AI platform to show its work when the product supports citations. You can also use this prompt: “Based only on the sources available in your answer, identify the sources that support the major claims about [COMPANY]. For each source, list the claim it supports, its publication date if available and whether newer authoritative information appears to conflict with it. Do not infer a source if you cannot identify one.”

Then open the sources. I consider this one of the most important steps in a modern reputation audit. Asking “How do we change this AI answer?” too early can send a company in the wrong direction.

Ask a better question: “Why does this information exist?” A factual problem at the source gives you something concrete to investigate.

AI has expanded reputation management, but it has not completely replaced traditional search yet.

Search your company name, executive names and relevant combinations such as your company plus “reviews,” “complaints,” “lawsuit” and other terms a prospective customer might reasonably use.

Look beyond position. A negative article does not become significant simply because it ranks highly. Determine its date, source, context and accuracy. Find out whether multiple independent sources support the underlying claim or whether dozens of pages repeat information originating from a single source.

The same principle applies to positive coverage. Ten websites repeating the same press release do not provide the same independent validation as 10 separate authoritative sources.

Your audit should measure the quality of the information surrounding your company, not simply count positive and negative links.

Review management creates another risk CEOs should examine. The Federal Trade Commission’s Consumer Reviews and Testimonials Rule took effect in October 2024. It addresses practices including fake or false reviews and incentives conditioned on a review expressing a particular positive or negative sentiment.

The FTC sent warning letters to 10 companies in December 2025 over potential violations of the rule and noted that violations can result in substantial civil penalties. Ask your marketing and customer service teams how they request reviews.

Are incentives involved? Does anyone ask specifically for a five-star review? Do employees write reviews? Does an outside vendor manage the process? Does anyone discourage dissatisfied customers from leaving legitimate feedback?

CEOs should understand the answers. I recommend one simple test: Could you comfortably explain your review-generation process to a regulator? If you hesitate, investigate it.

Finish the audit by creating a basic spreadsheet. You only need seven columns:

Run the same core questions every quarter and compare the findings.

Label accurate information and isolated criticism as issues to monitor. Investigate recurring inconsistencies, outdated information and unsupported claims. Prioritize consequential factual errors, impersonation and rapidly spreading false information for action.

Consistency matters more than complexity. The first audit tells you what your reputation looks like today. Repeating the process shows you where it is moving.

A company preparing for an acquisition, leadership change, product launch or other major event may need to run the audit more frequently. Most CEOs can start with a quarterly review and adjust based on the risks they uncover.

Your goal is not to make every search result positive or force every AI platform to praise your company. Neither goal is realistic. Your goal is to know what customers can discover about you, understand where that information comes from and correct factual problems where you legitimately can.

In 2026, people increasingly ask machines to help them evaluate businesses and the people running them. CEOs should know what those machines are finding before an important customer, employee or business partner asks.

Your customers can now investigate your company without visiting your website or clicking a traditional search result.

They can ask an AI platform to compare your company with competitors, summarize customer complaints, research your leadership and identify potential reasons not to do business with you. The resulting answer can shape an opinion before the customer reaches your website.

That changes what CEOs need to monitor. Google results, news coverage, reviews and social media still matter, but an online reputation audit in 2026 should also examine what AI platforms say about your business, which sources support those answers and whether inaccurate or outdated information keeps appearing.

#5441. Rand Fishkin’s Seattle game studio serves up first trailer for ‘The Snackbar at the End of the World’

by Kurt Schlosser on Nov 11, 2026 at 11:21 amNovember 11, 2026 at 11:21 am

If the eventual release of “The Snackbar at the End of the World” is a full-on meal for video game fans, news this week of the game’s first trailer should at least suffice as an appetizer.

Seattle-based Snackbar Studio, co-founded by SparkToro founder Rand Fishkin and his wife, writer Geraldine DeRuiter, unveiled its debut title and Steam page on Tuesday. The hand-drawn narrative adventure RPG puts players in the role of a chef trying to save a struggling family restaurant in a magical version of 1960s Italy.

The studio now plans to launch the game late next year, after originally targeting the second half of 2026. Snackbar raised $2.15 million from 38 angel investors two years ago, and the project began four years ago, according to Fishkin. The team includes five co-founders (Fishkin, DeRuiter, game designer Nicolas Kraj, lead programmer Miriam Cabrera and art director Francesco Mazza) plus about 10 contractors.

In the studio’s description on Steam, players forage for ingredients in the “forbidden wilds” outside town, battling explosive tomatoes, chaotic zucchini and vendetta-driven poultry. They then cook dishes back at the restaurant before a tyrannical mayor known as the Sindaco can shut it down. The game mixes combat and stealth with cooking mini-games based on real-world recipes.

The trailer is set to “’O surdato ’nnammurato,” a classic Neapolitan song performed by professional musicians recruited by the studio’s music director. Fishkin said he and DeRuiter both cried the first time they heard it.

Fishkin is best known in Seattle tech circles as co-founder of SEO software company Moz and audience research startup SparkToro, and he more recently launched Alertmouse, a tool for tracking online mentions. DeRuiter, a writer and author, is Snackbar’s head writer.

In a LinkedIn post this week, Fishkin recalled telling DeRuiter during the COVID lockdown that he wanted to fulfill a childhood dream of making a video game. Her reply: “Don’t wait. Do it now. I’ll do it with you.”

In the same post, he said the game’s themes include found family and fighting fascism “even when there’s no hope you’ll win.” He called it a love letter to DeRuiter’s small family village in the mountains outside Naples, to that era of Italy, to video games, and to the many people both of their families have lost in recent years.

Moments like hearing that song come often in the work, Fishkin said, such as when a new feature clicks or a new animation brings DeRuiter’s characters to life. He has always loved art without being good at any form of it. “I may not be able to create art, but I can enable it,” he said. “What a wonderful feeling.”

There have been lows, too. The team spent its initial 18 months on the project with a contract agency that didn’t work out, losing money with nothing to show for it. Fishkin is glad they kept going, “even when it felt financially irresponsible.”

The game is entirely human-made, and Snackbar’s no-AI stance is firm. “Geraldine hates AI with the fury of a thousand suns,” Fishkin said. He once suggested, just once, that she use Google’s AI Mode to find a synonym, and she was mad at him for the rest of a six-hour flight home from Philadelphia. Even if players, the rest of the team and the games media were fine with AI (and they’re not), DeRuiter alone would make it a no-go, he said.

Still ahead are 10 to 12 months of finishing the game’s content, playtesting, bug fixing, marketing and launch prep. Fishkin called it daunting, but said team members have done it many times before, “even though it’s our first rodeo.”

Fishkin is still juggling Snackbar with SparkToro and Alertmouse, and describes his role at the studio as mostly oversight and management. SparkToro is growing again, and Alertmouse recently hit a big milestone in annual renewals with high retention. He and his Alertmouse co-founders are putting more money into the company to fund growth.

Balancing the three roles is a challenge, he said, but only rarely completely overwhelming. “Like this week.”

#5440. ‘Chinese companies are born to make money’: AI pioneer Kai-Fu Lee on the 3 biggest myths about China’s AI race efforts

Despite years of U.S. efforts to gain an edge over China in the AI race by restricting its access to the most advanced chips, one AI pioneer says America’s efforts have instead helped create a new generation of Chinese AI models that are quickly catching up to their American counterparts.

Kai-Fu Lee, an AI entrepreneur and former president of Google China, said in a Fortune Daily interview that U.S. export restrictions on the most powerful American chips have shaped Chinese companies’ strategy of building competitive AI models with fewer resources.

In response to these limits, which American companies don’t face, Chinese AI developers have built open-weight models that Lee estimates are now just six to 12 months behind those created by some of the biggest American AI companies, including OpenAI as well as Anthropic—which is reportedly preparing to go public as early as next week.

Yet when Americans think about China and the motivations of Chinese companies, they’re often getting some key things wrong, Lee said. In an interview with Fortune Daily published this week, he detailed three of the biggest misconceptions about China’s AI industry that he says have taken hold in America.

One of the biggest misconceptions about Chinese companies is that they are more focused on winning the AI race and becoming the first to develop artificial general intelligence (AGI)—widely considered the ultimate goal of AI development—than on building profitable businesses. That assumption is incorrect, Lee said.

“Chinese companies are born to make money. That’s the primary purpose,” Lee said. “It’s not so much to win AGI or win the race.”

He compared questions about the profitability of the current wave of Chinese AI developers like DeepSeek with those surrounding other Chinese tech companies like Pinduoduo, Meituan, and ByteDance. These tech giants’ business models were also initially questioned before they became some of China’s biggest companies.

“You may reasonably doubt China’s ability to do a breakthrough, which is valid. [The] U.S. is way ahead on that, but never doubt Chinese ability to find a way to make money,” he said.

A second misconception, Lee said, is that China’s embrace of open-weight models and open-source technology is part of an organized government effort to compete with America.

Instead, Lee said, market competition has driven the shift. He pointed especially to DeepSeek, a Chinese startup that stunned American AI companies in early 2025 by releasing a highly capable AI model by the same name that it claimed was trained using significantly less computing power than its American competitors.

“Chinese companies are venture funded just like the American companies,” Lee said. “They just want to serve their investors.”

Beijing has played a significant role in shaping the country’s AI industry. Investors with ties to the government participated in more than 140 Chinese AI deals in 2025, Fortune reported earlier this year, citing a Pitchbook analyst note.

China’s president, Xi Jinping, has also encouraged AI development in China. In 2025, Xi called for the country to develop “an independent, controllable, and collaborative artificial intelligence basic software and hardware system.”

Lee said in the interview that American companies have good reasons to spend more, including attracting the world’s best researchers and giving them enough computing power to experiment.

The third misconception, Lee argued, is that U.S. export controls are the main reason Chinese companies have shifted toward models that require less computing power, while American companies pour billions into data centers.

He argued that Chinese companies are naturally more frugal because they have different priorities than their American counterparts.

“The Chinese companies are naturally parsimonious; not just the startups,” he said, adding that “prudence and survival instinct” are more important to them than the pursuit of AGI.

That contrasts with the American approach, which emphasizes spending heavily on computing power to attract top researchers and accelerate AI development. Because of their resourcefulness, Chinese companies can develop and operate models for as little as one-tenth the cost of their American competitors, making their products attractive to businesses that don’t want to pay premium prices for AI services.

Despite the growing competitiveness of Chinese AI developers, American companies still produce more top-tier models and higher-impact patents, according to a Stanford University study. OpenAI and Anthropic are also the world’s most valuable AI companies.

OpenAI was valued at $1.25 trillion in a November funding round and is eyeing a potential IPO in 2027. Anthropic, meanwhile, is preparing to go public as early as next week in what could be one of the largest IPOs in history, seeking a valuation of up to $1.4 trillion.

Still, when DeepSeek showed it could compete with America’s leading AI developers, it helped boost the hopes of Chinese AI developers. Before DeepSeek, these developers believed their country was years behind the U.S. After DeepSeek showed off its model in 2025, sentiment shifted, he said.

“It’s a national pride thing, so people say, ‘Okay, we thought we were never going to catch up. Now we have a shot.’ So, it was quite a special moment,” he said.

Role: Reporter Marco Quiroz-Gutierrez is a reporter for Fortune covering general business news.

#5439. Binance’s $6.3B Hack Fix Is Coming Tomorrow: Why the ZK Math Doesn't Tell the Whole Story

AI-assisted summary, reviewed by NullTX editors.

On-chain data shows the attacker behind the $6.3 billion Binance theft depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses.

At the same time, Binance's first post-hack reserve snapshot shows its biggest assets covered with buffers as small as 2.7 ETH and $6 of USDT. Binance's full zero-knowledge proof of those figures is due by Tuesday.

Some of the money stolen from Binance has started going back to Binance.

Blockchain intelligence firm Arkham has flagged the entity it tracks as "Binance Hacker" depositing about $4 million into three Binance deposit addresses. Arkham says those addresses "likely represent nested service(s)." These are third-party exchanges that use Binance for liquidity and custody, giving their own customers deposit addresses that sit on Binance's infrastructure.

If Arkham is right, the hacker isn't depositing into an ordinary Binance account. The money would be going to smaller platforms that operate through Binance. Exchanges have long known this is a weak point for stolen funds moving into normal trading. Either way, Binance is now receiving stolen funds at its own deposit addresses while it works to show customers it has replaced what was taken.

The FBI has attributed the October 29 theft to North Korea. The deposits come at a sensitive moment. Binance has just published its first reserve snapshot since the hack and has promised a full cryptographic proof of it by Tuesday.

$4 million is a small slice of a theft worth about $6.3 billion, but it matters for two reasons.

It shows how the laundering works. Nested services are a common way into the regulated financial system. A third-party platform that relies on Binance for custody may run weaker identity checks on its own users. Funds deposited there can be swapped and withdrawn without the hacker ever opening a Binance account.

Binance can act on it. Binance can't freeze bitcoin and ether sitting in wallets nobody controls, and it doesn't control the stablecoins that issuers like Tether and Circle have frozen. Deposits that land at its own addresses are different: they are on Binance's platform, so Binance can freeze them itself. One of the first tests of how Binance handles the money still in the hacker's hands is whether it freezes these funds and identifies the services that own the addresses.

While the hacker's funds move, Binance has been rebuilding its reserves. Its proof-of-reserves page now shows:

The first page covers Binance's six largest assets. Customer balances are what users hold. Reserves are on-chain wallet balances, including assets held with outside custodians.

The second page has four more assets, and two of them stand out:

Why USD1 and RLUSD matter: these are two of the stablecoins whose issuers froze stolen funds after the attack. World Liberty Financial froze $27 million of USD1, and Ripple began freezing RLUSD the same night. Both now show reserves above what Binance owes customers.

Assets with outside custodians: part of several reserves sits with outside custodians rather than in Binance's own exchange wallets:

The striking part isn't that the ratios reach 100%. It's how closely they stop there.

Compared with October's report: Binance's previous monthly report, published in early October before the hack, showed BTC at 100.35% and USDT at 103.88%. ETH was already at exactly 100.00%. After the theft:

Not every asset is that tight. USDC, ZEC and BNB carry buffers of 1.3% to 6%. The thinnest buffers are in BTC, ETH, USDT and SOL, which are among the assets the attacker took in the largest amounts.

How Binance says it got here: the pattern fits Binance's account of replacing the stolen assets in stages. It reported 80% replaced on Friday, 90% on Saturday and 95% on Sunday. The remaining 5% is in less-liquid tokens it is still buying. The money came from:

Binance confirmed taking 7,499 BTC from SAFU and has pledged to refill the fund to about $1 billion.

What the snapshot can't show: it was taken a little over a day after the theft, once the rebuild was under way. It shows the balance sheet after the replacement, not how large the gap was on October 29.

Binance says the full proof takes 40 to 50 hours to compute. Its latest update says it will be ready "by Tuesday, 2026-11-03 (UTC)." The system is open source, in Binance's zkmerkle-proof-of-solvency repository.

What the proof guarantees, according to the project's circuit design document:

The design also guards against a "dummy user attack" identified by Ethereum Foundation researcher Enrico Bottazzi. In that attack, fake accounts holding cheap tokens are used to offset debts in major assets.

What it doesn't prove: the reserve side. The project's verifier config describes the totals as information "published by CEX, it represents CEX's liability." The reserve figures are checked a different way, against the wallet addresses Binance publishes through the page's "Download All Address" option.

What customers can do: each user can get a Merkle proof for their account and check it against the published root. They can use the verifier code in Binance's repository rather than Binance's own interface. That doesn't prove Binance is solvent, but it confirms the user's balance was counted.

Binance has rebuilt its reserves to 100% across its ten largest assets, but on several of them the buffer is only a few coins. Meanwhile, stolen funds are reaching its deposit addresses through platforms that run on its infrastructure. Tuesday's proof can confirm customer balances. It can't show how Binance handles the stolen money arriving at its own door.

#5437. Lila Bio lands $3.65M grant to fight pulmonary hypertension with AI-designed proteins

by Lisa Stiffler on Nov 11, 2026 at 2:31 pmNovember 11, 2026 at 2:31 pm

Lila Bio, a startup spun out of Nobel laureate David Baker’s lab at the University of Washington, has received a $3.65 million grant from the National Institutes of Health to develop a treatment for pulmonary hypertension.

The condition causes high blood pressure in the arteries that carry blood from the heart to the lungs. It forces the heart to work harder and can lead to heart failure.

The Small Business Innovation Research fast-track award supports Lila’s efforts to develop a protein-based treatment for pulmonary hypertension that could be given by injection a few times a year.

“Most approved therapies only manage symptoms, such as vasodilators,” Lila CEO Jake Kraft said in a LinkedIn post, referring to drugs that widen blood vessels. “Lila Bio is pursuing clinically-validated, disease-modifying mechanisms that treat the underlying disease.”

The funding comes from the NIH’s National Heart, Lung, and Blood Institute and is divided into two phases. The initial $605,981 will support early testing in mice, rats and non-human primates. The second phase, totaling $3,049,462, will support further animal testing and studies using lung tissue from patients.

Kraft and chief scientist Anindya Roy co-founded Lila in 2023. Both worked as postdoctoral fellows at UW’s Institute for Protein Design, which Baker directs. Lila raised $10 million in seed funding the year it was founded. Last year, it announced a collaboration with pharmaceutical giant Eli Lilly to develop treatments for solid tumors.

The startup uses AI and machine learning to design therapeutic proteins through two platforms. One supports the pulmonary hypertension project, creating long-acting injectable drugs designed to remain active in the body for weeks or months. The other focuses on targeted radiotherapy, using proteins to deliver radioactive isotopes to tumors.

“We want to bring medicines to patients,” Kraft told GeekWire in an earlier interview. “We don’t want to just say we’ve designed a protein, but we actually want to be able to say we’ve saved lives.”

Uber received “preferred delivery partner” status as its delivery fight with DoorDash heats up.

McDonald’s is giving Uber the inside track. The Golden Arches named Uber its “preferred delivery partner” for orders placed through the McDonald’s app in 14 countries, including the U.S., U.K., Canada and France, Bloomberg reports. Up until now, McDonald’s split those orders between Uber and DoorDash.

For customers, the change is mostly behind the scenes. If you order in the McDonald’s app, an Uber driver will likely bring your Happy Meal. DoorDash announced plans to buy Instacart in late October, and Uber countered earlier this month with an Amazon Prime delivery deal.
